author: Theophilus of Alexandria
occasion: The fragments explain passages from Matthew, especially the parable of the two sons, applying them to the contrast between Gentiles and Israel and between true repentance and mere words.
argument: Theophilus interprets the parable of the two sons in Matthew 21:28–32. The first son represents the Gentiles, whom God as common Father called first by sowing the teachable and natural law in their minds and giving the visible creation as heralds, though their soul's good order was poured out onto wood and stones before they later repented and went into the vineyard. The second son represents Israel, called through Moses, who promised to do and hear all that God spoke but neither did nor heard nor repented afterward. Therefore repentant tax collectors and prostitutes, who were persuaded by John, are justified, while Pharisees who only speak of keeping the law are rejected, because the kingdom of heaven consists not in words but in deeds.

outline.move: The fragment opens with a warning that it is untimely to unfold deeper things to the deceitful who do not come to learn, then identifies the first son in the parable as the Gentiles, whom God called first by sowing the teachable and natural law in their minds and giving visible things as heralds, though their soul's good order was poured out onto wood and stones before they later repented and went into the vineyard.

After the first son refused, the father approached the second son, Israel, who when called through Moses said they would do and hear all that God spoke, but they neither did nor heard nor repented afterward, and the prostitutes and tax collectors, that is, the Gentiles, condemned them.
The parable means that tax collectors and prostitutes who repented and did what pleases God are justified by being persuaded by John, even if at first they disobeyed the law, or rather God.

Pharisees who claim to keep the law in bare words alone are rejected by God, because the kingdom of heaven is not in words but in deeds, and the doer of the law, not the hearer, is righteous; they are like those who promised to go work in the vineyard but did not go.

cast.name: The Father
cast.who: God, called the common Father when he called the Gentiles first; he calls both sons sequentially.

cast.name: The First Son
cast.who: Represents the Gentiles, called first through the natural law sown in their minds.

cast.name: John
cast.who: The one by whom tax collectors and prostitutes are justified through being persuaded by him.

cast.name: The Pharisees
cast.who: Those who claim to keep the law in bare words but are rejected by God.

voices.speaker: The Gentiles (as the first son)
voices.how_marked: Their speech is introduced by «εἶπαν», with γὰρ following; the quoted words are «τῷ ξύλῳ· πατήρ μου εἶ σύ» (to the wood: you are my father).

voices.speaker: Israel (as the second son)
voices.how_marked: Introduced by εἶπεν; the content is a composite scriptural quotation: «πάντα ὅσα ἐλάλησεν ὁ θεὸς καὶ ποιήσομεν καὶ ἀκουσόμεθα» (all that God spoke, and we will do and we will hear), echoing the Sinai response.

voices.speaker: Early Christian sayings or tradition
voices.how_marked: Quoted as sayings with γὰρ inside the quoted material: «οὐ γὰρ ἐν λόγοις ἡ βασιλεία τῶν οὐρανῶν, ἀλλ' ἐν ἔργοις» and «οὐ γὰρ ὁ ἀκροατὴς τοῦ νόμου, ἀλλ' ὁ ποιητὴς»; not directly identifiable Old Testament quotations.

key_terms.sense: The vineyard in the parable, representing the work God calls people to do.
The Gentiles, the non-Jewish nations, represented by the first son.
The people of Israel, represented by the second son.
To repent, to change one's mind and turn to God.
Tax collectors, a despised group who repented and were justified.
Prostitutes, a despised group who repented and were justified.
The law, especially the Mosaic law, and also the natural law given to the Gentiles.
To be justified, declared righteous by God.
The kingdom of heaven, which consists in deeds rather than words.
The Pharisees, who claim to keep the law in words only.
The good order or discipline of the soul, which in the Gentiles was poured out onto wood and stones.
The teachable and natural law that God sowed in the minds of the Gentiles.

scripture: The author cites Matthew by chapter and verse (e.g., Mt 21:23; Mt 21:28–32). Old Testament quotations appear without book names in the fragments; where identifiable, they should be cited using LXX book names and Psalm numbering, with modern equivalents noted as needed.
uncertain: The exact date of composition is unknown.
The original extent and structure of the commentary cannot be reconstructed from these fragments.
The precise source of the quotation 'οὐ γὰρ ἐν λόγοις ἡ βασιλεία τῶν οὐρανῶν, ἀλλ' ἐν ἔργοις' is uncertain; it may be a paraphrase or unattributed saying.
The identity of the addressee or original audience is not stated in the fragments.
The precise source of the saying 'οὐ γὰρ ὁ ἀκροατὴς τοῦ νόμου, ἀλλ' ὁ ποιητὴς' is uncertain; it resembles James 1:22 but may be an early Christian saying.

_unresolved_facts.fix: The one by whom tax collectors and prostitutes are justified, having been persuaded (by him). Note: The dative Ἰωάννῃ is instrumental ('by John'), but the text does not explicitly say John 'persuaded' them; rather they were persuaded and so justified.

_unresolved_facts.claim: and the prostitutes and tax collectors, that is, the Gentiles, condemned them
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: οὓς κατέκριναν αἱ πόρναι καὶ οἱ τελῶναι, τοῦτ' ἔστιν τὰ ἔθνη
_unresolved_facts.fix: whom the prostitutes and tax collectors, that is, the Gentiles, condemned. Note: The relative pronoun οὓς refers back to Israel/the second son (the ones condemned), not forward to the Gentiles. The brief reverses who condemns whom.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The parable means that tax collectors and prostitutes who repented and did what pleases God are justified by being persuaded by John, even if at first they disobeyed the law, or rather God.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: εἰ καὶ κατ' ἀρχὰς ἠπείθουν τῷ νόμῳ, μᾶλλον δὲ τῷ θεῷ
_unresolved_facts.fix: even if at first they disobeyed the law, or rather God. Note: The μᾶλλον δὲ correction applies to the object of disobedience (law → God), not to the subject; the brief's 'or rather God' could be read as correcting 'tax collectors and prostitutes' rather than 'the law'.
